Order-Preserving Extensions of Hadamard Space-Valued Lipschitz MapsThanks: This paper is in final form and no version of it will be submitted for publication elsewhere.

Edoardo Gargiulo Address: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, New York University Email address: eg3504@nyu.edu and Efe A. Ok Address: Department of Economics and Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, New York University Email address: efe.ok@nyu.edu
Date: January 25, 2026
Abstract.

We study the problem of extending any order-preserving Lipschitz function that maps a subset of a partially ordered Hilbert space XX into a Hadamard poset YY without increasing its Lipschitz constant and preserving its monotonicity. This sort of an extension is always possible when XX is one-dimensional. However, when dimX≥2\dim X\geq 2 and YY satisfies some fairly weak conditions, it holds (universally) if and only if the order of XX is trivial. The conditions on YY are satisfied by any Hilbert poset. Therefore, as a special case of our main result, we find that there is no order-theoretic generalization of Kirszbraun’s theorem.

Key words and phrases: 
Hadamard posets, partially ordered Hilbert spaces, order-preserving Lipschitz maps, radiality, Busemann functions, Kirszbraun’s theorem
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 54C20, 54C30; Secondary 06F30

1. Introduction

A pair (X,Y)(X,Y) of metric spaces has the Lipschitz extension property if for any nonempty S⊆XS\subseteq X and any 1-Lipschitz map f:S→Y,f:S\rightarrow Y, there exists a 1-Lipschitz F:X→YF:X\rightarrow Y that extends f.f. One of the central problems in Lipschitz analysis is to determine those (X,Y)(X,Y) that has the Lipschitz extension property.11 1 A stellar reference on this problem and its variants is Benyamini and Lindenstrauss [5]. Two classical results delineate the scope of this problem. The McShane-Whitney theorem (of [15] and [25]) asserts that (X,ℝ)(X,\mathbb{R}) has the Lipschitz extension property for every metric space X,X, while Kirszbraun’s theorem (of [12]) says (X,Y)(X,Y) has the Lipschitz extension property for every Hilbert spaces XX and YY.22 2 To be precise, Kirszbraun proved this for maps between two finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. Valentine [21] noticed that the theorem extends to the context of Hilbert spaces without modification. Some authors thus refer to this result as the Kirszbraun-Valentine theorem.

When metric spaces carry additional structure, it is natural to ask whether Lipschitz extensions can be obtained so as to preserve that structure. In particular, when the domain and the codomain are partially ordered metric spaces, one may require extensions to be order-preserving in addition to being Lipschitz. To be precise, we say that a pair (X,Y)(X,Y) of partially ordered metric spaces has the monotone Lipschitz extension property if for any nonempty S⊆XS\subseteq X and order-preserving 1-Lipschitz map f:S→Y,f:S\rightarrow Y, there is an order-preserving 1-Lipschitz F:X→YF:X\rightarrow Y with F|S=f.F|_{S}=f.33 3 The continuous version of this problem for real-valued maps (i.e., extending a monotonic continuous real function on a subset of a topological poset to the entire space monotonically and continuously) has received abundant attention. The literature on this problem has started with Nachbin [16], and found profound applications in decision theory, mathematical economics, and optimal transport theory. For recent contributions to this literature, see [26], and references cited therein.

Ok [18] has recently characterized the class of all partial orders on XX relative to which (X,ℝ)(X,\mathbb{R}) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property. As this class contains the equality relation on XX (which is unable to compare any two distinct points in the space), that result provides an order-theoretic generalization of the McShane-Whitney theorem.

The purpose of the present paper is to investigate to what extent the coverage of Kirszbraun’s theorem can be extended in this manner. We are thus particularly interested in the case where XX and YY are Hilbert posets (= Hilbert spaces vector ordered by means of pointed closed convex cones), but our main result not really linear, and it applies to a much richer class of metric spaces. We begin by observing that a positive result is readily obtained by affine interpolation when X=ℝX=\mathbb{R} and YY is any Banach poset (Theorem 2). When the dimension of XX exceeds 1, however, things change radically.

In the context of Hilbert spaces, the main result of this paper reads as:

The No-Extension Theorem. Let X=(X,≽X)X=(X,\succcurlyeq_{X}) be a partially ordered Hilbert space with dimX≥2\dim X\geq 2, and Y=(Y,≽Y)Y=(Y,\succcurlyeq_{Y}) any Hilbert poset. Then, (X,Y)(X,Y) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property if, and only if, ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} is trivial.

When ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} is trivial (that is, it is the equality relation), every map on XX is automatically order-preserving. Thus, in that case, the monotone Lipschitz extension property is identical to the Lipschitz extension property, so all reduces to Kirszbraun’s theorem. The no-extension theorem thus shows that there is no order-theoretic generalization of Kirszbraun’s theorem.

We obtain the no-extension theorem as a special case of a more general no-extension theorem in which YY belongs to a fairly large class of Hadamard posets. (A Hadamard poset is a complete CAT(0)-space endowed with a geodesically hereditary closed partial order; see Section 2.4.) At a heuristic level, the proof of this latter result rests on a simple, but rigid, obstruction mechanism that combines order structure of the domain with asymptotic geometry of the codomain. The key observation is that if order-preserving 1-Lipschitz extensions into a given Hadamard poset YY were universally possible, then the partial order on the domain XX would necessarily satisfy a strong metric compatibility condition, called radiality (Section 2.2). This necessity is detected by a test map on a two-point set whose order-preserving 1-Lipschitz extension forces a metric inequality via composition with a monotone Busemann function associated with an order-preserving geodesic ray in YY (Theorem 3). Thus, to obtain this necessity, we presume that YY possesses at least one monotone Busemann function associated with an order-preserving geodesic ray. This condition is met by any Hilbert poset (Proposition 10), among many other Hadamard posets (Examples 1-3).

It remains to explore how demanding radiality is. This property is fairly forgiving in the context of finite metric posets (cf. [18]). By contrast, we find here that it is extremely restrictive on connected metric posets (Theorem 4). In fact, if a metric space contains a copy of a close simple loop, such as a normed space with dimension ≥2,\geq 2, then it cannot be nontrivially radially ordered (Theorem 5). Putting these observations together yields a general result (Theorem 8), a special case of which is the necessity part of the no-extension theorem we stated above.

We conclude the paper by outlining a research agenda for studying the monotone Lipschitz extension problem quantitatively.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Posets

Let XX be a nonempty set. A preorder on XX is a reflexive and transitive binary relation on X,X, while a partial order on XX is an antisymmetric preorder on X.X. We refer to the ordered pair (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) as a poset if ≽\succcurlyeq is a partial order on X.X. Obviously, the smallest partial order on XX is {(x,x):x∈X};\{(x,x):x\in X\}; we refer to this partial order as the trivial order on XX. A preorder ≽\succcurlyeq on XX is total if any two elements xx and yy of XX are ≽\succcurlyeq-comparable, that is, either x≽yx\succcurlyeq y or y≽xy\succcurlyeq x holds. A total partial order on XX is said to be a linear order on XX.

In what follows, unless otherwise is explicitly stated, we regard ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} as a poset relative to the usual coordinatewise order. Obviously, this order is total iff n=1n=1.

Given any poset (X,≽),(X,\succcurlyeq), we denote the asymmetric part of ≽\succcurlyeq by ≻\succ, that is, x≻yx\succ y means y≠x≽y.y\neq x\succcurlyeq y. We also define the binary relation ≽∙\succcurlyeq^{\bullet} on XX as

x≽∙yiff   not y≽x.x\succcurlyeq^{\bullet}y\hskip 14.45377pt\text{iff\hskip 14.45377ptnot }y\succcurlyeq x.

Thus x≽∙yx\succcurlyeq^{\bullet}y means that either x≻yx\succ y, or xx and yy are not ≽\succcurlyeq-comparable. It is plain that ≽∙\succcurlyeq^{\bullet} is an irreflexive relation. In general, this relation is neither symmetric nor asymmetric, nor it is transitive. When ≽\succcurlyeq is total, however, ≽∙\succcurlyeq^{\bullet} equals ≻\succ.

A function f:X→Yf:X\rightarrow Y from a poset X=(X,≽X)X=(X,\succcurlyeq_{X}) to a poset Y=(Y,≽Y)Y=(Y,\succcurlyeq_{Y}) is said to be order-preserving (or isotonic) if for every x,y∈Xx,y\in X,

x≽Xyimplies f(x)≽Yf(y).x\succcurlyeq_{X}y\hskip 14.45377pt\text{implies\hskip 14.45377pt}f(x)\succcurlyeq_{Y}f(y).

If Y=(ℝ,≥),Y=(\mathbb{R},\geq), where ≥\geq is the usual order, we refer to ff simply as ≽\succcurlyeq-increasing.

2.2. Partially Ordered Metric Spaces

Let X=(X,d)X=(X,d) be a metric space. We say that (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) is a partially ordered metric space if ≽\succcurlyeq is a partial order on X.X. If, in addition, ≽\succcurlyeq is a closed subset of X×X,X\times X, we refer to (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) as a metric poset.

By a radially ordered metric space, we mean a partially ordered metric space (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) such that

(1) x≽∙y≻zimplies d(x,z)≥d(x,y)x\succcurlyeq^{\bullet}y\succ z\hskip 14.45377pt\text{implies\hskip 14.45377pt}d(x,z)\geq d(x,y)

and

(2) x≻y≽∙zimplies d(x,z)≥d(y,z).x\succ y\succcurlyeq^{\bullet}z\hskip 14.45377pt\text{implies\hskip 14.45377pt}d(x,z)\geq d(y,z)\text{.}

(In this case, we refer to the partial order ≽\succcurlyeq on XX as radial.) This concept will play an essential role in our analysis of the monotonic Lipschitz extension problem.

The trivial order on XX is obviously radial. [18] provides several other examples of radial orders on a metric space.

Remark. Radial partial orders were introduced in Ok [18] who showed that the property of radiality is necessary and sufficient for all order-preserving 1-Lipschitz real-valued maps on a subset of a partially ordered metric space to be extendable to such maps on the entire space. As such, it is not surprising that it will play an important role for the present work, but the role of radiality here will be a bit more nuanced. It may be worth noting that every radially ordered metric space (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) is radially convex, that is, d⁡(x,z)≥max⁡{d⁡(x,y),d⁡(y,z)}d(x,z)\geq\max\{d(x,y),d(y,z)\} holds whenever x≻y≻z.x\succ y\succ z.44 4 Radially convex metric posets are studied in topological order theory (cf. [4], [6] and [23], among many others). They are also used in the topological analysis of smooth dendroids; (cf. [9]). The converse is false, but a linearly ordered metric space is radial if and only if it is radially convex.

It may come as a small surprise that every radial partial order is closed. This was proved in [18] in a very indirect manner. As we will need it below, we give an elementary proof of this fact.

Lemma 1. Every radially ordered metric space (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) is a metric poset.

Proof. Take any x,x1,x2,…,y,y1,y2,…∈Xx,x_{1},x_{2},...,y,y_{1},y_{2},...\in X such that xm≽ym,x_{m}\succcurlyeq y_{m}, xm→x,x_{m}\rightarrow x, and ym→y.y_{m}\rightarrow y. To derive a contradiction, suppose x≽yx\succcurlyeq y is false. Let us distinguish between two cases. First, suppose x≽ymx\succcurlyeq y_{m} for infinitely many m.m. Then, there is a subsequence (ymk)(y_{m_{k}}) of (ym)(y_{m}) such that y≽∙x≽ymky\succcurlyeq^{\bullet}x\succcurlyeq y_{m_{k}}, so, by radiality, d⁡(x,y)≤d⁡(y,ymk),d(x,y)\leq d(y,y_{m_{k}}), for all k≥1k\geq 1. Letting k→∞k\rightarrow\infty here yields x=y.x=y. Second, suppose x≽ymx\succcurlyeq y_{m} holds for at most finitely many m.m. Then, for some M∈ℕM\in\mathbb{N}, we have xm≽ym≽∙xx_{m}\succcurlyeq y_{m}\succcurlyeq^{\bullet}x for all m≥Mm\geq M. Thus, by radiality, d⁡(x,ym)≤d⁡(x,xm)d(x,y_{m})\leq d(x,x_{m}) for all m≥M,m\geq M, so letting m→∞m\rightarrow\infty yields x=yx=y once again. We conclude that y≽∙xy\succcurlyeq^{\bullet}x implies x=y,x=y, contradicting the reflexivity of ≽\succcurlyeq. ■\blacksquare

Let X=(X,‖⋅‖)X=(X,\left\|\cdot\right\|) be a normed (real) linear space. We say that (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) is a partially ordered normed space if ≽\succcurlyeq is a vector order on X,X, that is, it is a partial order on XX such that x≽yx\succcurlyeq y implies λ​x≽λ​y\lambda x\succcurlyeq\lambda y for all λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and x+z≽y+zx+z\succcurlyeq y+z for all z∈X.z\in X. If, in addition, ≽\succcurlyeq is a closed subset of X×X,X\times X, we refer to (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) as a normed poset. The terms partially ordered Banach/Hilbert space and Banach/Hilbert poset are understood accordingly.

The positive cone of any partially ordered normed space (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) is defined as C⁡(≽):={x∈X:x≽𝟎}C(\succcurlyeq):=\{x\in X:x\succcurlyeq\mathbf{0}\} where 𝟎\mathbf{0} denotes the origin of X.X. As it contains 𝟎,\mathbf{0}, this set is always nonempty. As is well known, C⁡(≽)C(\succcurlyeq) is a pointed convex cone in XX such that x≽yx\succcurlyeq y iff x−y∈C⁡(≽)x-y\in C(\succcurlyeq).55 5 As a reminder, we note that a convex cone in a linear space XX is a subset CC of XX such λ​C⊆C\lambda C\subseteq C for all λ≥0,\lambda\geq 0, and C+C⊆C.C+C\subseteq C. Such a cone is said to be pointed if C∩−C={𝟎}C\cap-C=\{\mathbf{0}\}. (Conversely, for every pointed convex cone CC in X,X, the binary relation ≽C\succcurlyeq_{C} on XX with x≽Cyx\succcurlyeq_{C}y iff x−y∈C,x-y\in C, is a vector order on XX.) Obviously, ≽\succcurlyeq is trivial iff C⁡(≽)={𝟎}C(\succcurlyeq)=\{\mathbf{0}\}. Moreover, if (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) is a normed poset, C⁡(≽)C(\succcurlyeq) is closed in XX.

2.4. Hadamard Posets

Let (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) be a metric poset. If XX is uniquely geodesic, and ≽\succcurlyeq is geodesically hereditary, that is,

x≽yimplies ​x≽z≽y​ for every ​z∈[x,y]​,x\succcurlyeq y\hskip 14.45377pt\text{implies\hskip 14.45377pt}x\succcurlyeq z\succcurlyeq y\text{ for every }z\in[x,y]\text{,}

where [x,y][x,y] is the geodesic segment between xx and y,y, we say that (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) is a geodesic poset. If, in addition, XX is a Hadamard space, that is, it is a complete CAT(0) space – this entails unique geodicity – we say that (X,≽)(X,\succcurlyeq) is a Hadamard poset. It is plain that every Hilbert poset is a Hadamard poset.

2.5. Lipschitz Functions

Let X=(X,≽X)X=(X,\succcurlyeq_{X}) and Y=(Y,≽X)Y=(Y,\succcurlyeq_{X}) be two partially ordered metric spaces, and f:X→Yf:X\rightarrow Y any function. For any real number K>0,K>0, we say that ff is KK-Lipschitz if dY​(f⁡(x),f⁡(y))≤K​dX​(x,y)d_{Y}(f(x),f(y))\leq Kd_{X}(x,y) for every x,y∈Xx,y\in X. (Here, and in what follows, dXd_{X} stands for the metric of X,X, and similarly for dYd_{Y}.) We say that ff is Lipschitz if it is KK-Lipschitz for some K>0.K>0. For excellent treatments of the general theory of Lipschitz functions, see [3], [7], and [24].

We denote the set of all KK-Lipschitz maps from XX to YY as Lip(X,Y)K,{}_{K}(X,Y), but write Lip(X)K{}_{K}(X) for Lip(X,ℝ)K.{}_{K}(X,\mathbb{R}). In turn, the sets of all order-preserving members of Lip(X,Y)K{}_{K}(X,Y) and Lip(X)K{}_{K}(X) are denoted as Lip(X,Y)K,↑{}_{K,\uparrow}(X,Y) and Lip(X)K,↑,{}_{K,\uparrow}(X), respectively.

2.6. The Monotone Lipschitz Extension Property

Let X=(X,≽X)X=(X,\succcurlyeq_{X}) and Y=(Y,≽Y)Y=(Y,\succcurlyeq_{Y}) be two partially ordered metric spaces. We say that (X,Y)(X,Y) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property if for every nonempty S⊆XS\subseteq X and f∈f\in Lip(S,Y)1,↑,{}_{1,\uparrow}(S,Y), there exists an F∈F\in Lip(X,Y)1,↑{}_{1,\uparrow}(X,Y) with F|S=f.F|_{S}=f. In this terminology, the classical McShane-Whitney extension theorem says: Provided that ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} is trivial, (X,ℝ)(X,\mathbb{R}) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property. Ok [18] has generalized this theorem as: (X,ℝ)(X,\mathbb{R}) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property if, and only if, ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} is radial.

Again using this jargon, we can state Kirszbraun’s theorem as follows: Provided that XX and YY are Hilbert spaces, and ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} is trivial, (X,Y)(X,Y) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property. This is a famous generalization of the McShane-Whitney theorem. The primary objective of the present paper is to figure the extent to which one can relax the triviality requirement on ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} in this statement.

By the monotone Lipschitz extension problem relative to two partially ordered metric spaces XX and YY, we understand determining if (X,Y)(X,Y) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property.

3. A Possibility Theorem

Let us first consider the monotone Lipschitz extension problem in a very specific case, namely, when X=ℝX=\mathbb{R}. In that setup, the partial order on XX is either trivial or linear. In the former case all maps that are defined on any subset of XX are automatically order-preserving (regardless of the codomain), so the problem reduces to a standard Lipschitz extension problem. (As the proof of Theorem 2 shows, such an extension is indeed possible, at least when YY is a Banach space.) In the latter case too all is well.

Theorem 2. Let Y=(Y,≽)Y=(Y,\succcurlyeq) be a Banach poset. Then, (ℝ,Y)(\mathbb{R},Y) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property.

We can prove this by affine interpolation. For brevity, we will only sketch the basic argument. Let SS be any nonempty set of the reals, and take any order-preserving 1-Lipschitz f:S→Yf:S\rightarrow Y. For any t1,t2,…∈St_{1},t_{2},...\in S with tm→t,t_{m}\rightarrow t, the Lipschitz property readily entails that (f⁡(tm))(f(t_{m})) is Cauchy in Y,Y, so as YY is Banach, (f⁡(tm))(f(t_{m})) converges in YY. (Again by the Lipschitz property, the limit depends only on t,t, not the sequence (tm).(t_{m}).) We may then define F:F: cl(S)→Y(S)\rightarrow Y by F⁡(t):=limf⁡(tm),F(t):=\lim f(t_{m}), where (tm)(t_{m}) is any sequence in SS with tm→tt_{m}\rightarrow t. It is plain that FF is 1-Lipschitz. The closedness of ≽\succcurlyeq ensures that FF is order-preserving as well.

It is thus without loss of generality to assume SS is closed. If S=ℝ,S=\mathbb{R}, there is nothing to prove, so we take SS as a nonempty closed proper subset of ℝ\mathbb{R}. Then, there exists a countable collection ℐ\mathcal{I} of disjoint nonempty open intervals with ℝ\S=⋃ℐ\mathbb{R}\backslash S=\bigcup\mathcal{I}. For any (a,b)∈ℐ(a,b)\in\mathcal{I} with a,b∈ℝ,a,b\in\mathbb{R}, we define

F⁡(t):=f⁡(a)+t−ab−a​(f⁡(b)−f⁡(a)),a<t<b.F(t):=f(a)+\frac{t-a}{b-a}(f(b)-f(a)),\,\,\,\,\,a<t<b.

If SS has a minimum element, say, a∗a_{\ast}, then (−∞,a∗)∈ℐ,(-\infty,a_{\ast})\in\mathcal{I}, and we set F⁡(t):=f⁡(a∗)F(t):=f(a_{\ast}) for all −∞<t<a∗-\infty<t<a_{\ast}. Dually, if SS has a maximum element, say, a∗a^{\ast}, then (a∗,∞)∈ℐ,(a^{\ast},\infty)\in\mathcal{I}, and we set F⁡(t):=f⁡(a∗)F(t):=f(a^{\ast}) for all a∗<t<∞a^{\ast}<t<\infty. This defines the YY-valued map FF everywhere on ℝ\mathbb{R}. It is routine to verify that FF is order-preserving and 1-Lipschitz.

4. Necessity of Radiality

It turns out that, under fairly general conditions, a pair of a partially ordered metric spaces XX and YY cannot have the monotone Lipschitz extension property unless XX is radially ordered. We will use this fact as a springboard for the main results of this paper.

5. Radial Orders on Connected Spaces

Theorem 3 witnesses the importance of radiality for the monotone Lipschitz extension problem. We are thus naturally led to investigate how demanding the radiality property is. While [18] provides quite a few examples of radially ordered metric spaces, those are not particularly suitable for the present setup, as they are all disconnected. In this section we will show that this is not accidental. It turns out that there is a considerable tension between connectedness of a metric space and its radial orderability.

Theorem 4. Let X=(X,≽)X=(X,\succcurlyeq) be a radially ordered metric space. If XX is connected, then ≽\succcurlyeq is either trivial or total.

Proof. Assume that XX is connected, and take an arbitrary x∈Xx\in X. We define x↑:={y∈X:y≽x}x^{\uparrow}:=\{y\in X:y\succcurlyeq x\} and x↓:={y∈X:x≽y}.x^{\downarrow}:=\{y\in X:x\succcurlyeq y\}. As ≽\succcurlyeq is closed (Lemma 1), it is plain that these are closed subsets of XX. We claim that both x↑\{x}x^{\uparrow}\backslash\{x\} and x↓\{x}x^{\downarrow}\backslash\{x\} are open in X.X. To see this, take any y∈x↑,y\in x^{\uparrow}, distinct from xx, and towards a contradiction, suppose yy is in the boundary of x↑\{x}x^{\uparrow}\backslash\{x\}. Then, there is a sequence (ym)(y_{m}) in X\x↑X\backslash x^{\uparrow} with ym→y.y_{m}\rightarrow y. Consequently, y≻x≽∙ym,y\succ x\succcurlyeq^{\bullet}y_{m}, so by radiality, d⁡(x,ym)≤d⁡(y,ym),d(x,y_{m})\leq d(y,y_{m}), for all m.m. Then, letting m→∞m\rightarrow\infty yields x=y,x=y, contradicting yy being distinct from x.x. This proves that x↑\{x}x^{\uparrow}\backslash\{x\} is open in X.X. Openness of x↓\{x}x^{\downarrow}\backslash\{x\} is proved analogously. As xx was arbitrarily chosen in X,X, and XX is connected, Schmeidler’s theorem (of [20]) yields our claim. ■\blacksquare

The second alternative envisaged in Theorem 4 fails in myriad cases. To wit:

Theorem 5. Let XX be a connected metric space that contains a copy of the circle 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}. Then, the only radial order on XX is the trivial order.

Proof. Let ≽\succcurlyeq be a radial order on XX. By Theorem 4, ≽\succcurlyeq is either total or trivial. To derive a contradiction, suppose the former case holds. Then, where f:𝕊1→Xf:\mathbb{S}^{1}\rightarrow X is an embedding, we define the binary relation ⊵\trianglerighteq on 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1} by a​⊵​ba\trianglerighteq b iff f⁡(a)≽f⁡(b).f(a)\succcurlyeq f(b). As ≽\succcurlyeq is closed (Lemma 1), ⊵\trianglerighteq is a closed linear order ⊵\trianglerighteq on 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}. Without loss of generality, we may assume eπ​i​⊵​1.e^{\pi i}\trianglerighteq 1. By closedness of ⊵\trianglerighteq, the set {θ∈[0,π]:e(θ+π)​i​⊵​eθ​i}\{\theta\in[0,\pi]:e^{(\theta+\pi)i}\trianglerighteq e^{\theta i}\} is a closed, hence compact, subset of ℝ\mathbb{R}. It thus contains its supremum, say, θ∗\theta^{\ast}. Clearly, θ∗<π\theta^{\ast}<\pi because otherwise, 1=e2​π​i​⊵​eπ​i,1=e^{2\pi i}\trianglerighteq e^{\pi i}, contradicting the antisymmetry of ⊵\trianglerighteq. It follows that

e(θ∗+π)​i⊵eθ∗​i and e(θ∗+ε)​i⊵e(θ∗+ε+π)​ie^{(\theta^{\ast}+\pi)i}\trianglerighteq e^{\theta^{\ast}i}\text{ \thinspace\thinspace and \thinspace\thinspace}e^{(\theta^{\ast}+\varepsilon)i}\trianglerighteq e^{(\theta^{\ast}+\varepsilon+\pi)i}

for arbitrarily small ε>0.\varepsilon>0. This contradicts ⊵\trianglerighteq being closed. ■\blacksquare

Remark. This proof is based on the observation that there is no closed total order on any connected metric space that contains a closed simple loop. The latter condition in this observation, and hence in Theorem 5, can be relaxed quite a bit. See, for instance, [17] and [22].

We now extract some concrete cases out of Theorem 5. First, let us agree to call a geodesic space XX nonbranching if for any geodesics σ:[0,1]→X\sigma:[0,1]\rightarrow X and σ′:[0,1]→X\sigma^{\prime}:[0,1]\rightarrow X with σ|[0,ε)=σ′|[0,ε)\sigma|_{[0,\varepsilon)}=\sigma^{\prime}|_{[0,\varepsilon)} for some ε>0,\varepsilon>0, we have σ=σ′.\sigma=\sigma^{\prime}. (For instance, every strictly convex normed space is nonbranching, but an ℝ\mathbb{R}-tree is not.) As usual, if XX is uniquely geodesic, we denote the geodesic segment between any two points xx and yy in XX by [x,y],[x,y], and set (x,y):=[x,y]\{x,y}.(x,y):=[x,y]\backslash\{x,y\}.

Corollary 6. Let XX be a nonbranching and uniquely geodesic space. Then, either XX is isometric to an interval, or the only radial order on XX is the trivial order.

Proof. We distinguish between two cases. First, assume that every distinct three points in XX are collinear (in the sense that one of these points lies in the geodesic segment between the other two points). Fix any distinct a,b∈X,a,b\in X, and define τ:X→ℝ\tau:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R} by

τ⁡(x):={d⁡(a,x),if ​x∈[a,b]​ or ​b∈[a,x],−d⁡(a,x),if ​a∈[x,b]​.\tau(x):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}d(a,x),&\text{if }x\in[a,b]\text{ or }b\in[a,x],\\ -d(a,x),&\text{if }a\in[x,b]\text{.}\end{array}\right.

Now take any distinct x,y∈X.x,y\in X. Without loss of generality, suppose τ⁡(y)≥τ⁡(x).\tau(y)\geq\tau(x). If τ⁡(x)≥0,\tau(x)\geq 0, then x∈[a,y],x\in[a,y], so d⁡(a,x)+d⁡(x,y)=d⁡(a,y),d(a,x)+d(x,y)=d(a,y), whence τ⁡(y)−τ⁡(x)=d⁡(a,y)−d⁡(a,x)=d⁡(x,y).\tau(y)-\tau(x)=d(a,y)-d(a,x)=d(x,y). Moreover, if both τ⁡(y)\tau(y) and τ⁡(x)\tau(x) are negative numbers, the same argument applies. Finally, suppose τ⁡(x)<0<τ⁡(y)\tau(x)<0<\tau(y). In this case, a∈[x,y],a\in[x,y], so d⁡(x,a)+d⁡(a,y)=d⁡(x,y),d(x,a)+d(a,y)=d(x,y), so τ⁡(y)−τ⁡(x)=d⁡(a,y)−(−d⁡(a,x))=d⁡(x,y).\tau(y)-\tau(x)=d(a,y)-(-d(a,x))=d(x,y). We conclude that d⁡(x,y)=|τ⁡(x)−τ⁡(y)|d(x,y)=\left|\tau(x)-\tau(y)\right| for all x,y∈X.x,y\in X. It follows that τ\tau is an isometry from XX into ℝ\mathbb{R}. As XX is geodesic, hence connected, τ⁡(X)\tau(X) is an interval. Thus, XX is isometric to an interval.

Finally, suppose there exist distinct points a,b,c∈Xa,b,c\in X that are not collinear. In this case (a,b),(a,b), (b,c)(b,c) and (a,c)(a,c) must be pairwise disjoint. (For instance, if dd belongs to (a,b)∩(a,c),(a,b)\cap(a,c), we must have [a,d]⊆[a,b][a,d]\subseteq[a,b] and [a,d]⊆[a,c][a,d]\subseteq[a,c] by unique geodicity, but as b≠c,b\neq c, this contradicts XX being nonbranching.) It follows that S:=[a,b]∪[b,c]∪[a,c]S:=[a,b]\cup[b,c]\cup[a,c] is a closed simple loop in XX which is, of course, homeomorphic to 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}. By Theorem 5, therefore, the only radial order on XX is the trivial one. ■\blacksquare

The following is a special case of Corollary 6.

Corollary 7. Let X=(X,≽)X=(X,\succcurlyeq) be a radially ordered normed space. Then, either dimX=1\dim X=1 or ≽\succcurlyeq is trivial.

Remark. The no-extension theorem we have stated in the Introduction is based on Corollary 7. It may thus be useful to give a direct, alternative proof for this result that does not rely on Schmeidler’s theorem. Suppose dimX≥2,\dim X\geq 2, and to derive a contradiction, assume ≽\succcurlyeq is not trivial. Put C:=C⁡(≽)C:=C(\succcurlyeq), the positive cone of XX. We begin with showing that CC has a nonzero boundary point. Suppose otherwise, so C\{𝟎}C\backslash\{\mathbf{0}\} is an open set. As ≽\succcurlyeq is radial, it is closed (Lemma 1), and this entails CC is closed. It follows that C\{𝟎}C\backslash\{\mathbf{0}\} is a clopen set in X\{𝟎}.X\backslash\{\mathbf{0}\}. But, as dimX≥2,\dim X\geq 2, X\{𝟎}X\backslash\{\mathbf{0}\} is path-connected, hence connected. Thus, either C\{𝟎}=∅C\backslash\{\mathbf{0}\}=\varnothing or C\{𝟎}=X\{𝟎}C\backslash\{\mathbf{0}\}=X\backslash\{\mathbf{0}\}. In the former case we get C={𝟎},C=\{\mathbf{0\}}, contradicting the nontriviality of ≽,\succcurlyeq, and in the latter case C=X,C=X, contradicting the antisymmetry of ≽\succcurlyeq. We conclude that there is a nonzero point yy in the boundary of CC. Let us now pick any sequence (ym)(y_{m}) in X\CX\backslash C with ym→yy_{m}\rightarrow y. Then, −ym∈X\−C-y_{m}\in X\backslash-C and −y∈−C,-y\in-C, that is, −ym≽∙𝟎≽−y-y_{m}\succcurlyeq^{\bullet}\mathbf{0}\succcurlyeq-y, for all m≥1m\geq 1. By radiality, then, ‖−ym‖≤‖−ym+y‖\left\|-y_{m}\right\|\leq\left\|-y_{m}+y\right\| for all m≥1.m\geq 1. Letting m→∞m\rightarrow\infty yields ‖y‖≤0,\left\|y\right\|\leq 0, that is, y=𝟎,y=\mathbf{0}, a contradiction. ■\blacksquare

6. Impossibility Theorems

Combining Theorem 3 and Corollary 6 yields the main result of this paper:

Theorem 8. Let X=(X,≽X)X=(X,\succcurlyeq_{X}) be a partially ordered, nonbranching and uniquely geodesic space, and Y=(Y,≽Y)Y=(Y,\succcurlyeq_{Y}) a partially ordered metric space. Suppose XX is not isometric to an interval, and there exists an order-preserving geodesic ray σ:[0,∞)→Y\sigma:[0,\infty)\rightarrow Y whose Busemann function is ≽Y\succcurlyeq_{Y}-decreasing. If (X,Y)(X,Y) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property, then ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} is trivial.

The converse is false at this level of generality.77 7 We thank Urs Lang for pointing this fact to us. A pair of nonbranching Hadamard spaces may well fail to have the Lipschitz extension property. For a simple example, take the Poincare disk, and any equilateral triangle on it. Map the corners of this triangle to an equilateral triangle (with same side lengths) on the plane isometrically. This map cannot be extended to a 1-Lipschitz map on the Poincare disk.

Corollary 9. Let X=(X,≽X)X=(X,\succcurlyeq_{X}) be a partially ordered Hilbert space with dimX≥2\dim X\geq 2, and Y=(Y,≽Y)Y=(Y,\succcurlyeq_{Y}) a Hadamard poset with an order-preserving geodesic ray whose Busemann function is ≽Y\succcurlyeq_{Y}-decreasing. Then, (X,Y)(X,Y) has the monotone Lipschitz extension property if, and only if, ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} is trivial.

Proof. We only need to prove the sufficiency, but this is a special case of Theorem A of Lang and Schroeder [13]. ■\blacksquare

We next show that the conditions of Corollary 9 are satisfied by any Hilbert poset YY.

Combining Corollary 9 and Proposition 10 yields the no-extension theorem we stated in the Introduction.

We conclude our exposition by noting that the generality afforded by Theorem 8 may be useful in other instances as well. The following simple examples aim to demonstrate this.

Example 1. (ℝ\mathbb{R}-tree-valued maps) Let YY be an ℝ\mathbb{R}-tree, that is, YY is a uniquely geodesic metric space such that for every a,b,c∈Ya,b,c\in Y with [a,b]∩[b,c]={b},[a,b]\cap[b,c]=\{b\}, we have [a,b]∪[b,c]=[a,c].[a,b]\cup[b,c]=[a,c].99 9 See [1] and [8] for nice introductions to the theory of ℝ\mathbb{R}-trees. 7. Concluding Comments

Let us restate the no-extension theorem of the Introduction in the common jargon of the recent literature on Lipschitz extensions. Let X=(X,≽X)X=(X,\succcurlyeq_{X}) and Y=(Y,≽Y)Y=(Y,\succcurlyeq_{Y}) be metric posets, and for any k∈ℕ∪{∞}k\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}, let 𝒳k\mathcal{X}_{k} denote the collection of all S⊆XS\subseteq X with 0<|S|≤k0<\left|S\right|\leq k. For any nonempty S⊆XS\subseteq X, define e↑(X,S,Y):=inf{K∈(0,∞]:e_{\uparrow}(X,S,Y):=\inf\{K\in(0,\infty]: for every f∈f\in Lip(S,Y)1,↑{}_{1,\uparrow}(S,Y) there is an F∈F\in Lip(X,Y)K,↑{}_{K,\uparrow}(X,Y) with F|S=f},F|_{S}=f\}, and for any k∈ℕ∪{∞}k\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}, define

ek,↑​(X,Y):=supS∈𝒳ke↑​(X,S,Y).e_{k,\uparrow}(X,Y):=\sup_{S\in\mathcal{X}_{k}}e_{\uparrow}(X,S,Y).

In the case where ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} is trivial (so Lip(S,Y)1,↑={}_{1,\uparrow}(S,Y)= Lip(S,Y)1{}_{1}(S,Y) for all S∈𝒳S\in\mathcal{X}), we write e⁡(X,Y)e(X,Y) for e↑,∞​(X,Y),e_{\uparrow,\infty}(X,Y), and ek​(X,Y)e_{k}(X,Y) for ek,↑​(X,Y)e_{k,\uparrow}(X,Y) for any k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}.

Quite a bit is known about the quantities e⁡(X,Y)e(X,Y) and ek​(X,Y)e_{k}(X,Y). For one thing, the McShane-Whitney theorem says e⁡(X,ℝ)=1e(X,\mathbb{R})=1 – in fact, e⁡(X,ℓ∞)=1e(X,\ell_{\infty})=1 – whereas Kirszbraun’s theorem says e⁡(X,Y)=1e(X,Y)=1 when XX and YY are Hilbert spaces. In a famous paper, Johnson and Lindenstrauss [10] have shown that ek​(X,Y)≤2​log⁡ke_{k}(X,Y)\leq 2\sqrt{\log k} when YY is a Hilbert space. In the case where YY is a Banach space, Johnson, Lindenstrauss and Schlechtman [11] have proved that ek​(X,Y)=O⁡(log⁡k),e_{k}(X,Y)=O(\log k), and Lee and Naor [14] have improved that estimate to ek​(X,Y)=O⁡(log⁡klog⁡log⁡k).e_{k}(X,Y)=O(\frac{\log k}{\log\log k}). Remarkably, these fascinating results are all obtained by probabilistic methods.1010 10 There are powerful estimates that bound ek​(X,Y)e_{k}(X,Y) from below as well. See [2] to learn about the state of the art in this area of research.

Very little is known in the order-theoretic setup, however. Ok [18] shows that e↑​(X,ℝ)=e↑​(X,ℓ∞)=1e_{\uparrow}(X,\mathbb{R})=e_{\uparrow}(X,\ell_{\infty})=1 when ≽X\succcurlyeq_{X} is radial, but we have found in this paper that radiality is excessively demanding in the case of connected metric spaces. We have e↑​(ℝ,Y)=1e_{\uparrow}(\mathbb{R},Y)=1 whenever YY is a Banach poset, but this is little comfort. For instance, we even have e↑​(ℝ2,ℝ)>1.e_{\uparrow}(\mathbb{R}^{2},\mathbb{R})>1. More generally, the no-extension theorem of the Introduction shows that when XX and YY are Hilbert posets with dimX≥2,\dim X\geq 2, we have e↑​(X,Y)>1e_{\uparrow}(X,Y)>1. In fact, our proof of this result shows that e2,↑​(X,Y)>1e_{2,\uparrow}(X,Y)>1 in this case. It should thus be quite interesting to seek upper bounds for the quantity ek,↑​(X,Y)e_{k,\uparrow}(X,Y) when XX and YY are arbitrary Hilbert posets (with dimX≥2\dim X\geq 2), but this will very much depend on the structure of the partial orders of XX and YY. For instance, as e↑​(X,ℝ)=1e_{\uparrow}(X,\mathbb{R})=1, we have e↑​(X,ℝn)≤ne_{\uparrow}(X,\mathbb{R}^{n})\leq\sqrt{n} for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} (where XX is any metric poset), but we do not presently know if this is the best upper bound, nor have good estimates for e↑,k​(X,ℝn)e_{\uparrow,k}(X,\mathbb{R}^{n}).
